summary: Very long observation of a luminous phenomenon in the sky: lack of precision and information.
description: On November 20, 1954, between 12:30 a.m. and 3:30 a.m., several people observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky. Only one witness account was recorded. The witness described a UFO (Unidentified Floating Object) moving vertically in a zigzag pattern from the south-southeast in a cloudless sky. The UFO was sometimes bright, sometimes dark, with a halo. This prolonged observation of a large point of light in the sky initially suggested an astronomical phenomenon: the star Sirius was observed in the southeast at 12:30 a.m., subsequently moving south. The halo may have been caused by an atmospheric haze from the desert sands. The zigzag pattern could be caused by the autokinetic illusion (a common perceptual illusion when observing a point of light in darkness). The observation direction is not described precisely enough to confirm this hypothesis (azimuth roughly estimated to SSE without change over time, elevation expressed in meters instead of being estimated in degrees). Lacking precise information regarding the position in the sky, GEIPAN classifies this case as C: lack of information.

summary: Observations similar to the evolution of a luminous color phenomenon: lack of information.
description: On October 31, 1954, around 8:00 PM, a farmer (T1) and his employee (T2) in a tractor observed a luminous phenomenon about twenty meters from their path as they entered a pasture. T1 described it as "a luminous object rotating a few meters above the ground." T2 described it as "a fireball spinning about 4 meters above the ground" with "beams of various bright colors surrounding it." T1 turned off the tractor's lights, and the witnesses saw the object rise obliquely at a normal speed towards the south, crossing the Somme River valley. When the witnesses turned the headlights back on, the object reappeared, spun again, and moved off towards the southwest. The shocked witnesses saw no trace of it on the ground. The next day, the farmer told the deputy mayor that the object was "circular in shape, about the diameter of an ordinary round table," and that he had heard "the same buzzing sound as a bee leaving its hive." The colors he saw were orange, with a blue center that made him close his eyes for a moment, and a brighter upper section. The gendarmerie learned of this sighting through the press and interviewed the witnesses, taking their statements on November 4th. The gendarmes were taken to the site of the sighting, but they found no trace in the grass. The police investigation also led to the discovery of two other witnesses: a shopkeeper in Long (T3) who observed, on the same day and at the same time, "an orange ball" emitting "glows of various colors similar to the glow of arc welding," "about a meter in diameter," and moving southwest "quite rapidly." A butcher (T4) reported to the police that he had seen above the trees bordering the Somme River "a cylindrical object" which, as it moved southwest, "became elongated, almost oval," and "emitted several orange glows." A few moments later, these two individuals saw the first two witnesses arrive, their faces contorted with fear. This case of observation, with two groups of two witnesses in two different locations within the town, is very strong. There is no doubt about the existence of the phenomenon. Several aspects of the phenomenon suggest ball lightning: a swirling, multicolored, and blinding appearance, and a sound like a swarm of bees. However, we lack sufficient information to confirm this hypothesis (weather conditions experienced by witnesses, weather records from that time). GEIPAN classifies this as case C due to a lack of meteorological data.

summary: Observation of the silent movement and evolution of a white-yellow cigar: lack of cross-checks.
description: On October 27, 1954, at approximately 11:15 PM, a witness walking along the RN 40 highway spotted an opalescent glow about ten meters ahead. It was a cigar-shaped craft, its front appearing wider than its rear, measuring 8 meters long and 0.80-1 meter in diameter, with no windows or doors. It moved silently at about 30 km/h at a height of 20 meters above the road, following its curves. It emitted a yellowish-white light confined to the craft's contours and not illuminating the rooftops of the houses it flew over. It disappeared around a curve in the road, reappeared further on, and then abruptly veered to its left (southwest) at the entrance to the town of Marck, 5 km away. It then appeared motionless, spherical, with a more intense and yellowish glow. The witness returns home, prepares his meal, and observes the object again in the same spot, but after eating, the object has disappeared. Despite the witness's efforts to get someone else to witness the phenomenon, he is the only one to make this observation. This observation is of moderate consistency, coming from only one witness who appears to be acting in good faith. What he describes is not very strange, as it is simply a point of light observed from a considerable distance. The object's movements are only observed when the witness moves: upon arriving home, he perceives the object as stationary. Several hypotheses are possible: - a very distant light, low on the horizon, which therefore appears to follow the witness's movements; an astronomical check indicates only the planet Mars in the witness's direction of observation, but it sets at 11 p.m. A light from the port of Calais is also a possibility. - a helicopter spotlight could have produced the same effect. GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to a lack of cross-checking.

summary: Observations of the evolution in the sky of a bright segment: probable observation of an aircraft illuminated by the setting sun.
description: On Wednesday, October 27, 1954, at the Mailly camp (in the commune of Mailly-le-Camp), two people, including a colonel, observed a very bright segment against the clear blue-green sky at around 5:45 PM, "slightly to the north of the setting sun" (2 to 3 minutes after sunset). The object was located at an angular altitude of 45° to 20° and was described as remaining stationary for 10 to 15 seconds, with a total observation time of 25 to 30 seconds. This segment, resembling bright metal, was inclined at 30° to the vertical and then suddenly became a point of light for 3 seconds before disappearing. Its size was between one-third and one-half the diameter of the Moon, or 10' to 15'. Only the colonel's testimony was recorded in an observation report, and some explanations in the handwritten report are illegible. The witness believes he likely saw an aircraft turning, illuminated from below by the setting sun. This type of observation, common nowadays due to heavy air traffic, can be seen every evening under clear skies shortly after sunset. GEIPAN classifies this case as B: probable sighting of an aircraft illuminated by the setting sun.

summary: Observations of a shower of sparks preceded by a detonation. Detection of a whistling and humming sound moving away to the NE: lack of information and corroboration.
description: On October 27, 1954, returning from a night shift, two gendarmes riding their bicycles with all lights off around 5:15 a.m. were exchanging a few words aloud about a white creature they had seen in the grass on the right side of the road. They were then surprised to hear a bang and immediately see, on the left side of the road, about 150 meters away, a shower of sparks 1 to 5 meters long, 1 to 1.5 meters above the ground, accompanied by a whistling sound followed by a humming noise. The noise quickly moved to the northeast. The gendarmes saw no shape. They approached but found nothing but frightened cows mooing. The gendarmerie investigation at the time recounts that the brigade commander went to the site with one of the witnesses at 7:45 a.m., and that the section commander did the same with the other witness at 1:30 p.m.; the two accounts from the two witnesses, thus collected independently, are in no way contradictory. On site, the gendarmes observed that the grass was flattened over an area of 1.6 by 1.3 meters and that a fence located 3.5 meters from this spot was torn up over a length of 25 meters (4 posts were damaged, 2 of which were broken at ground level). Neither the landowner nor the gendarmes believed that this damage was caused by livestock. The grass could have been flattened by cows before or after the observation. It is not certain that the marks on the ground are related to the phenomenon heard. A detonation followed by a shower of sparks and a whistling sound obviously suggests the explosion of a pyrotechnic device. The observation took place in a geographical area traversed by various armies during different wars. Could the self-ignition of an abandoned military explosive have produced this type of phenomenon without leaving a crater? It is surprising that the gendarmes considered the traces on the ground as the landing of an unidentified craft when they observed no such shape. Could this idea have been influenced by the particularly intense media frenzy surrounding flying saucers in October 1954? GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to a lack of information and corroboration.

summary: Observations of the silent north-south passage of a luminous trail in the sky: probable observation of the passage of a bolide.
description: On October 21, 1954, at 7:30 PM, two gendarmes observed, for no more than 15 seconds, a very bright luminous trail silently crossing the sky at high speed in a north-south direction. In the dark night with a clear sky and visible stars, this trail was shaped like a crescent moon, with its point forward and its base extended by numerous sparks. Its trajectory was horizontal. Although the witnesses (wrongly) ruled out a meteor due to its size and the horizontality of its trajectory, this is probably what they saw. GEIPAN classifies this case as B: probable observation of a fireball caused by the reentry into the atmosphere of a natural meteoroid that fragmented.

summary: Observations of the evolution of a luminous colored phenomenon in the sky before disappearance: unidentified phenomenon.
description: On Tuesday, October 19, 1954, between 1:30 and 1:40 a.m., several military personnel (including a private, a corporal, and a sergeant) from a radar station in Doullens (the radar was not operational that night) observed an unusual aerial phenomenon on a dark night, located beneath a continuous layer of stratocumulus clouds (estimated base at 1000 m). The observation had three phases: Phase 1: The luminous green phenomenon appeared at 1:34 a.m. above a farm to the east-northeast (Mondicourt direction), emerging from the clouds at an angle of 45° to the vertical, then moved horizontally eastward at an altitude of 45° over 90° (text) or 120° (plan) in half a second, without noise, changing color (green to orange, then dull red). This phase was apparently only seen by the sentry in his hut located on the embankment in front of the radar station. Phase 2: the phenomenon stopped abruptly above La Bellevue (eastward direction) at an angular height of 60 arcseconds (estimated altitude 800 m). This stationary position lasted 2 (sergeant) to 3 (private) minutes, allowing the sentry to alert his superiors. The object stood out clearly against the cloud layer with an angular size of approximately 1 arcsecond. To the sergeant, it had a disc shape, the lower surface of which was visible, but it traced an ellipse inclined at 25-30 arcseconds to the horizontal. It emitted a light that changed color approximately every 5 seconds: from a pale green to orange and then yellow (sergeant), while maintaining a greenish background (private). It oscillates (sergeant) or moves horizontally and vertically (private). Phase 3: the phenomenon moves in the opposite direction to its arrival at high speed and disappears into the clouds for 30 seconds, reappears for a few seconds (sergeant) or 2 minutes (private), then disappears again. The moon, in this cloudy sky, is to the east (azimuth 84°) and could be a source of confusion: it is in the direction of observation given by the witnesses (NE). Moreover, it was very close to Jupiter that evening (a separation of approximately 2.5 arcseconds), which was particularly bright (magnitude -1.78). In addition, the witnesses do not mention the moon in their field of vision. However, the color changes and perceived movements are difficult to explain under this hypothesis. The flight of an airplane does not seem compatible with a stop of several minutes at a constant angular size. A helicopter could also be considered; the color variations would be due to the alternating visibility of the left and right position lights (red and green). However, the very high speeds observed do not fit this hypothesis well. If the altitude of 800 m (deduced from the cloud ceiling estimated at 1000 m) is correct, the distance of the phenomenon during phase 2 is on the order of 1 km and its size 15-20 m (1e). This case of medium consistency, quite strange although distant, is classified as D1: unidentified strange phenomenon.

summary: Observations of a luminous phenomenon with rainbow colours: lack of information.
description: On October 14, 1954, at approximately 5:00 PM, four witnesses observed a spherical object moving silently at very high speed in a southwesterly direction at an altitude of 40 meters. The object displayed rainbow colors. GEIPAN received a brief information report without witness statements. The description of a very fast, multicolored spherical object suggests a fireball. This overly brief case is classified as Class C due to a lack of information.

summary: Long observations of an orange disc shaped like an upside-down plate; disappearance to the NW: lack of information.
description: On October 9, 1954, around 8:00 PM, three farmers observed an orange disc in the sky, shaped like an inverted plate, for 45 minutes. It disappeared in a northwesterly direction. The observation was briefly reported in an intelligence message from the National Gendarmerie. The duration of the observation and the described shape suggested possible confusion with the Moon. The Moon was indeed visible in the sky, but to the southeast and at an elevation of almost 30 degrees, which did not correspond at all to the context of the observation. GEIPAN classified this case as Category C due to a lack of information.

summary: A luminous, circular object was observed in the sky. The phenomenon is moving east-west: lack of information.
description: On October 8, 1954, at 11:30 PM, four witnesses observed a luminous, circular object in the sky. The phenomenon was moving east-west. The observation lasted a few seconds. This observation was recorded in a brief report by the National Gendarmerie. This type of observation can have various origins (sunlight reflection on an aircraft, balloon, fireball). GEIPAN classified this case as Category C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observations of the movement of a very bright, oval-shaped, aluminum-colored object in the sky: lack of information.
description: On October 7, 1954, at 9:00 AM, two people observed a bright, oval-shaped, aluminum-colored object directly above the church steeple. The object was moving from southeast to northwest. The observation lasted one minute. The National Gendarmerie recorded a brief report on this sighting. This type of observation can have various origins (sunlight reflection on an aircraft, balloon, fireball). GEIPAN classified this case as Category C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation of a luminous disk moving very slowly: probable observation of a scientific balloon.
description: On October 6, 1954, around 8:00 PM, several members of a family observed a luminous, reddish-orange disc from their home for approximately 40 minutes. The disc's apparent diameter was about half that of the full moon, and it appeared to be supporting a kind of gondola. The light intensity varied, flashing on and off alternately. The object appeared to be located above Senlis and was moving slowly to the right. GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) received a brief information sheet from the gendarmerie. Only one witness statement was recorded. At the time of the observation, the sun had set half an hour earlier; it still illuminated high-altitude objects such as airplanes or scientific balloons. The shape described by the witnesses and the westward direction of observation supported this interpretation. GEIPAN classified this case as B: probable observation of a scientific balloon.

summary: child observes a machine on the ground and a being: lack of information.
description: On October 4, 1954, between 6:40 and 7:00 PM, a 10-year-old girl (T1) riding her bicycle saw a contraption about 20 meters away, which she initially mistook for a camping tent. According to the child, the oval-shaped contraption was about 2 meters wide and 2.5 to 3 meters high, with a conical top, and rested on the ground on a rectangular base. As she approached the contraption, a hatch (1 x 0.6 meters) opened. A man jumped out, closed the hatch behind him, and then stood motionless. He was of average height, had a square-shaped head, piercing eyes, and wore a long, reddish-brown fur garment. When the man moved forward, the frightened child ran away without looking back. Two other people reported seeing the object at the same time and in the direction the girl was located. One reported a bright red light, which he ignored, while the other reported the sound of a skimmer, which prompted her to leave her house. The child's father and a neighbor went to the location of the sighting at 9:00 PM that same day and noted that the grass was slightly ruffled in a circular pattern. The police went to the site on October 6th but were unable to make any findings. No further details were gathered during the investigation. In summary, there are four distinct events in this case: - a single witness who saw an object and a person near her path. She did not see the object take off. - simultaneously, a farmer saw a bright red light in the sky. - a third person heard a noise resembling that of a skimmer for a long time. -The child's father and a farmer found, at 9 p.m. that same evening, at the T1 observation site, crumpled grass arranged in a circular pattern. No conclusive evidence guarantees that these four events are related. If we consider them to be related, we can propose a hypothesis to consider: -several elements seem consistent with a helicopter, perhaps a Bell 47, viewed from the front (oval shape): the rotor support, the hatch, the noise, the rustling of the grass, the pilot. The location (on a grassy path leading into a small clearing) could be suitable for a landing. However, the rectangular base, the position of the hatch (if it had been on the side, would the witness have been able to note its width?), and the bright red light of the object are less easy to interpret. This case is of moderate strangeness, as a simple hypothesis could be considered a reasonable explanation. Its consistency is weak, relying primarily on a single witness (a child) and a brief observation period. GEIPAN classifies this case as category C due to a lack of information and corroboration.

summary: Quick observation of the SW-NE movement of a very bright elliptical object in the sky: lack of information
description: On October 2, 1954, a witness was preparing to photograph a dolmen around 4:00 PM in sunny weather when he spotted a light-colored, elliptical object moving southwest-northeast. He took two photos and sent the negatives to the magazine "Radar e." The gendarmerie learned of the event through the press and did not meet with the witness until October 15. The prints were only included in the first mailing of the report (no photos were included with the copies of the report available to GEIPAN). A brief investigation into this case was conducted by GEIPAN in the late 1970s. It concluded that the photos were not published in the magazine "Radar e" and that the search for the witness (who was about 58 years old at the time) had been unsuccessful. The observation lasted only a few seconds, just long enough to take two photos in quick succession. The phenomenon disappears before the witness has time to adjust their camera settings. The overly brief description and the absence of photos prevent analysis of this observation; GEIPAN classifies this case as category C.

summary: Observation of several phenomena in two days in the same municipality: lack of information.
description: On October 2nd and 4th, 1954, several residents of the commune of Poncey-sur-l'Ignon (21) witnessed phenomena that intrigued them. The official report details two distinct series of events in the same area, presented here chronologically. The first event took place on October 2nd, 1954, in Poncey-sur-l'Ignon. At 7:40 PM, a farmer (T6), who had just finished milking her cows, first noticed in the sky "a luminous object" "related to everything we've been seeing in the press lately." The witness reported seeing something like a moonbeam that "lit up the yard." She thought it was the Moon but discovered that it had a strange shape. Focusing her attention, the witness then observed a vertical cylinder, which she estimated to be 1.5 meters high and 80 centimeters in diameter. It was luminous across its entire surface, orange with a greenish sheen, and moved upright at a low altitude, rather close to buildings. Convinced it was not the Moon but an unknown "craft," she alerted her husband, son, and a neighbor (T7). They had time to see the light, coming from the north, disappear toward the south. The neighbor (T7) described a luminous sphere like a soccer ball, more orange than a light bulb, and moving silently. Confusion with the Moon, perhaps partially obscured by moving clouds, cannot be ruled out despite the witness's denials. The Moon was indeed very low on the horizon (6°) in the southwest (azimuth 220°). In her testimony, witness T6 did not specify her exact location or direction of observation ("in the sky"); furthermore, she did not indicate having seen both the Moon and the "craft." Witnesses describe a slow-moving, southward movement, but the description of the disappearance is too vague. However, the phenomenon presents similarities with other reports two days later in the same town (see below). This first case is classified as Class C due to lack of information. The second series of events took place on October 4, 1954, in Val d'Ignon, at a place called "the asbestos factory," 1 km south of the village of Poncey-sur-l'Ignon (21). This place consists of a group of buildings, part of which houses three workers' families. It is surrounded to the north, east, and west by meadows and to the south by a pond. Around 7:30 p.m., as she was closing her bedroom shutters, a young woman (T1) saw, to the north, above a plum tree in the courtyard, a rather bright, yellowish light, seemingly mushroom-shaped, oval at the top and round at the bottom, appearing as a transparent globe lit from within. She estimated its height at about fifteen meters, its distance at 50 meters, and compared its size to that of a cook. No particular noise is heard. She only looks at it for a few moments and cannot determine its state of movement. Panicked, she grabs her child and seeks refuge at a neighbor's house (T2) who is alone with her daughter (T3). No other witness observes this phenomenon. Around 8:30 p.m., the neighbor's son-in-law (T4) and son (T8) arrive and find the three women frightened. Together they go to the meadow adjoining the courtyard, in the direction from which T1 observed the phenomenon. They note the presence of an approximately rectangular area (1.50 x 0.50-0.70 m) dug into the ground (to a depth of 5 cm) with broken earth at both ends and clods of earth and grass scattered around it in a circle with a radius of about 4 m. The clods are of unequal sizes (generally 30 x 20 cm except for two measuring 60 cm). cm) are turned grass downwards. Two witnesses (T2 and T4) report the presence of numerous live white worms among the tracks. Around 8:45 p.m., the neighbor's second son (18 years old) (T5), returning from work in the neighboring village 1.5 km away, briefly glimpses in the sky a wingless, cigar-shaped craft, entirely luminous, transparent in color with green and orange reflections, crossing the sky very quickly in a North-South direction. Frightened by this sight, he quickly returns home to his parents. No other witness observes this phenomenon. The gendarmes are notified on October 5th at 7:30 p.m. and observe the tracks on the ground that same evening. They conduct an investigation and compile the photographic record on October 6th, 1954. They consider the possibility of a prank by the neighbor's son-in-law and son (especially since, upon returning the On the evening of the 4th, they intended to play a prank about a flying saucer! But after checking their schedule, the police rejected this hypothesis. According to T4, who lives in the neighborhood, no livestock was grazing in the meadow, and he hadn't seen anyone return to that area the day before. A quick examination of the facts suggests four hypotheses for this second sighting: for the luminous phenomenon, the moon or a vehicle's headlight on the neighboring hill; and for the marks on the ground, either wild boars digging for worms or a hoax. The moon was indeed quite low on the horizon (elevation 16°). However, it was in the south (azimuth 197°). Yet the official report specifies that the sighting was made towards the north. A precise reconstruction of the location based on photographs (see reconstruction map) confirms that it was not a mistake and that the The window through which the witness made their brief observation clearly faces north. The moon hypothesis is ruled out. The headlight of a vehicle on the D26 road or in the bend of the D103 could have been visible from the witness's location to the north (see the 1963 IGN map, which shows that the vegetation cover is sparse). However, this hypothesis cannot be confirmed due to a lack of knowledge of the precise location of the observation and the exact direction of the phenomenon. A private investigator visited the site in August 2015 to try to clarify the topography of the observation: the area has changed little, but the inhabitants from 1954 no longer live there or have passed away. GEIPAN attempted to contact one of the witnesses by telephone and mail, but without success. Regarding the tracks on the ground, the wild boar hypothesis does not appear to be consistent with the descriptions of the excavation: relatively clean edges, Clods of earth were deposited outside the excavation, fairly regular in size and position (upside down), with uneaten white worms (the wild boars may have been disturbed). Photographs of the tracks taken by the gendarmerie were taken two days after the observation. Furthermore, these tracks were trampled by the witnesses. This hypothesis remains plausible but unconfirmed. The possibility of a hoax perpetrated by others cannot be completely ruled out. Can the light phenomenon be considered the cause of the tracks? The available data provides no direct proof of a cause-and-effect relationship. We must be content with the correlation in the direction of observation of the two phenomena (light and tracks on the ground) and the relative correlation in time within a one-hour interval. A similar question applies to the observations of 7:30 p.m. and 8:45 p.m. (T5), but with a weaker association: a distance of approximately 1-1.5 km between the witnesses (the exact location of the observation). The time of 8:45 PM is not precise) and the separation was approximately one hour. The agreement between the descriptions (yellowish or orange light, impression of transparency) remains limited. There is also a certain similarity between the observations of October 2nd and 4th: same town, same time of day, same light (orange with green reflections, with green and orange reflections), same apparent size (cooker, 1.8 x 0.8m, trace 1.50 x 0.60m). In summary, the observation case of October 4, 1954, reports three events: two distinct, short observations, each by a single witness, of a distant luminous phenomenon. Then, traces on the ground. These three events are not necessarily related. For each of these events, there are fragile hypotheses that cannot be confirmed. Overall, the consistency of this case is average because it does not contain of verifiable elements. Its strangeness would be significant if the ground markings and luminous phenomena could be definitively correlated. GEIPAN therefore classifies this case as C due to a lack of information: the verifiable elements are too weak compared to the supposed strangeness of the case. Note: it should be noted that during 1954, and particularly in October, the national and local press published a large number of articles reporting alleged UFO sightings. This widespread phenomenon made a strong impression on the population and generated numerous reports of observations of phenomena that ultimately proved to be very commonplace (stars, planets, airplanes, fireballs). In this police report, the various witnesses frequently refer to what they have recently read in the press, particularly to describe the phenomenon.

summary: pilot's distant observation of the movement of a circular object: lack of information.
description: On October 2, 1954, an experienced pilot (approximately 10,000 flight hours, a specialist in flying in the Alps), piloting a Nord 1203, was flying on a heading of 250°, at 220 km/h and an altitude of 2,000 m. At 4:20 PM, he observed an object to his right moving on the same heading at an altitude of approximately 4,000 m, located at a distance he estimated to be about 10 km. Its trajectory followed an upward curve. Its shape was that of a disc tilted on its axis at a 30° to 40° angle, with a phosphorescent glow on its rear edge. Its diameter was estimated at 3-4 m. It disappeared over the horizon after 70 seconds. The pilot made a brief report of his observation. No other witness statements were collected. The sun (azimuth 245°, site 18°) is aligned with the flight path. The aircraft travels approximately 4,300 m during the observation. The object is seen at an elevation of about 11° at an azimuth close to 340° (no astronomical confusion was identified in this area; see the star chart). It follows an ascending trajectory and then disappears below the horizon, indicating that the witness failed to describe the descending portion. The witness interprets what they see as a disk inclined at 30-40° to its axis, but which axis is it? One could imagine a disk whose front is lower than its back (or vice versa), or whose left edge is lower than its right (or vice versa). In the latter case, the object would have the shape of an ellipse. Does the witness have objective reasons for describing a disc tilted at an angle, or is it simply an interpretation? Furthermore, the angular size of the object is very small, since an object 3-4 m in diameter at a distance of 10 km is seen at an angle of 1' to 1.4' (0.15 to 0.2 mm at arm's length), which is the limit of the eye's resolution (in high contrast and luminance). The pilot, flying on a heading of 250°, is almost directly into the sun (azimuth 244°, elevation 18°): a reflection of the sun on a much closer, small object (a balloon) or even a reflection of the sun on the canopy cannot be ruled out. GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to a lack of information and corroboration.

summary: Observations by children of a small character and a "flying crate": lack of information and cross-checking.
description: On September 27, 1954, at approximately 8:40 a.m., three children (aged 10, 8.5, and 5) were walking to school on National Route 13 east of Ceint-d'Eau (Figeac, Drôme) when they encountered a small figure who fired a shot, frightening them. The two older children had previously noticed a kind of crate in the meadow bordering the road. Both children reported that the crate had quickly disappeared: the older child at noon, and the younger one around 8:40 a.m. The schoolteacher notified the gendarmerie. The children were interviewed by the gendarmes the following morning. The gendarmerie found no traces on the ground. No other witness statements were collected. GEIPAN classifies this case as Category C due to a lack of information, contradictory reports, and insufficient corroboration.

summary: Observations by children of a moving craft nearby; observation of a red glow and traces on the ground: lack of information.
description: On September 27, 1954, at 8:30 p.m., three children (aged 12, 9, and 8) observed a strange, rectangular, aluminum-colored object near their house. The object was partially split lengthwise down the middle. On each side of its base, the object had two externally angled supports. It measured approximately two meters high by one meter wide. One of the children threw a stone and then a dart from a toy he had at the object, which moved slowly forward and knocked the child over. Frightened, the child went home and lay down. Two sisters also saw the object and, frightened, went to hide. No one witnessed the object disappear. The two sisters also reported seeing a red glow swaying close to the ground near their house. The parents did not believe the children's accounts. Their teacher reported the sighting to the police. During the police investigation at the time, two reports were drawn up. The captain did not question the children's credibility. They lived on an isolated farm, did not read newspapers, and did not go to the cinema. Traces were found on the ground in the direction from which the red glow appeared: a large ring in the grass, lying flat and oriented clockwise. These traces were not recognized as being from trampling by people or animals. Four holes were also found in this ring. GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) learned of the investigation by private ufologist Yves Bosson, who met with the witnesses in the 1980s. The witnesses confirmed that they had played a prank whose consequences had escaped them. His report was presented at the Lyon Congress in 1992 ("Proceedings of the Sixth European Meetings of Lyon, May 1-2-3, 1992", SOS OVNI, Aix-en-Provence 1992, pp. 4-16), then published in the chapter "Premanon or Innocence: Investigation into a Case Above All Suspicion", in the book "UFOs, Towards an Anthropology of a Contemporary Myth", by Thierry Pinvidic et al., Heimdal publisher, France, pp 123-145, 1993. Pending verification of these claims, which are a priori reliable, GEIPAN classifies this case as C: lack of confirmed information.

summary: Observations of a circular object on the ground with an oscillating movement. Silent takeoff at an angle then vertically, emitting smoke; no trace on the ground: strange unidentified phenomenon.
description: On September 7, 1954, at approximately 7:30 a.m., two witnesses were cycling to work on local road 47 between Harponville (80) and Contay (80). The weather was clear and fog-free. They observed a circular shape in a field 200 meters from the road, exhibiting an oscillating motion. The two witnesses described it as a dark-colored cylinder with a slightly domed top and an opening around its circumference. Intrigued, the witnesses approached to within about 100 meters and saw the object silently rise diagonally for about 15 meters, then vertically. During its ascent, the witnesses noticed bluish-gray smoke escaping from a pipe. The observation lasted between four and five minutes before the phenomenon disappeared into the sky. The frightened witnesses immediately went to the gendarmerie. Later that same day, the investigation found no trace of the object in the field. One of the witnesses, having previously seen helicopters, stated that this was not such an aircraft. No other witness statements were collected. The credibility of the witnesses was not questioned. GEIPAN classified this case as D1: strange unidentified phenomenon.

summary: Observation of the movements of a dark teche in the sky; sudden changes of direction and disappearance over the sea on the horizon: lack of information.
description: On Sunday, September 5, 1954, at 5:15 PM, a couple and their daughter, located near the PTT radio transmitter near Cape Spartel (Morocco), observed a circular black spot, approximately the size of an airplane, high in the sky. One of the witnesses reported that for 10 minutes he was able to follow the movements of this dark phenomenon, heading south. No light, smoke, or sparks were observed. No noise was heard. The movements were punctuated by abrupt stops. The phenomenon disappeared westward, diving towards the sea until it vanished over the horizon. Only one witness account was collected, along with a map and diagram. The hypothesis that the aircraft originated from the Rabat-Salé air base (home of the 8th Fighter Wing, equipped with Vampire aircraft) and was performing aerobatics is plausible. The fixed points could correspond to the moment the witness saw the aircraft head-on. However, the lack of information regarding the object's angular size and its disappearance over the sea towards the horizon prevents us from fully confirming this hypothesis. GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to insufficient information.

summary: Observation of the fall of a luminous orange disc: lack of information.
description: In 2012, a witness reported an observation made in July or August 1954 around 8 p.m. (see questionnaire) in Sainte-Clotilde (municipality of Mers-el-Kébir) near Oran, Algeria; the witness was 15 years old at the time. He later placed the observation on a weekday between August 24th and 27th. In Saint-Clotilde, one evening, people sitting at a table were suddenly surprised to see a very bright, bright orange disc fall from the sky. It followed a downward trajectory towards the sea but stopped in mid-air and remained motionless above the horizon. The disc then accelerated at high speed on an upward trajectory at a 45° angle to the east before disappearing. The observation lasted approximately two minutes. Only one witness account of this phenomenon was collected. However, an article in Le Provençal dated August 27, 1954, reports a fireball sighting from Plan-de-Cuques (13) on August 22, 1954, at 8:00 PM. The fireball hypothesis could explain a large part of the observation described in this case. However, given the numerous uncertainties surrounding this case—the precise date unknown, the memory being old and therefore potentially altered, and the second part of the observation only explainable by an unverifiable physiological cause—GEIPAN classifies this case as C, indicating an unusable observation, due to a lack of reliable information.
